content: Vital heat, also referred to as innate or natural heat (calidum innatum), is a term historically used to describe the heat generated within the body, primarily by the heart and the circulatory system. Ancient Greek physicians believed that this vital heat originated in the heart, was sustained by the pneuma (interpreted as spirit or soul), and was distributed throughout the body via blood vessels. These vessels were thought to function as intact tubes that transmitted heat through the movement of blood. Aristotle supported this concept by demonstrating that when the heart becomes colder than other organs, death ensues. He theorized that the heat produced by the heart caused the blood to behave similarly to boiling liquid, expanding outward through the blood vessels with each heartbeat. However, he also posited that this intense heat could lead to a self-consuming flame if it were not regulated and cooled by air drawn in from the lungs. Galen, in his work On the Usefulness of the Parts of the Body (170 CE), described the heart as the hearthstone and source of the innate heat by which the animal is governed. This idea was later echoed in the 11th century by Avicenna, who, in his Canon of Medicine, agreed that the heart was the origin of breath and the vital power or innate heat that sustained the body.
